<meta>continues from previous page: and with the bellows</meta>stirs up the fire: in this way both the receiving pit <note>original: "catinus"</note> and the hearth <note>original: "focus"</note> are sufficiently heated within the space of half an hour. Certainly, if ore <term>uena</term> was smelted in the same furnace the previous day, they heat up more quickly; if it was not smelted, they heat up more slowly. Truly, if the hearth and receiving pit are not heated before the ore to be smelted is thrown in, they will cause a defect in themselves and damage to the metals. For if the dust from which both are made was damp in the summer time, or frozen in the winter, both will burst along with the metals and other contents, sending out a sound like thunder and scattering, not without great danger to the men.

Then the master should throw the slags <term>recrementa</term> into the furnace; once melted, these will flow from the mouth into the receiving pit. Soon he should block the mouth with clay with which charcoal dust has been mixed. He applies this by hand to a round wooden pestle, five fingers thick and two palms high, whose handle is three feet long. Then he should extract the slags from the receiving pit with a hooked pole. If he is about to smelt rich gold or silver ore, he should place a hundred-weight of lead into it; if poor ore, half as much. For he has need of much lead for the former, and little for the latter. Soon he should throw firebrands over the lead so that it melts. After this, he should do everything according to custom and throw things into the furnace in a certain order: first, such a portion of cakes melted from pyrites <term>pyrite</term> as is needed to smelt the ore; then, as much of the ore mixed with silver-dross <term>spuma argenti</term> <gloss>litharge</gloss>, <term>molybdæna</term> <gloss>lead oxide or galena</gloss>, and stones of the second kind that melt easily in the fire as two troughs can hold; then as many charcoals as a trough woven from wooden strips can contain; and finally, the slags.

With the furnace now filled with the aforementioned things, he should gradually smelt the ore; but he should not throw it too close to the rear wall of the furnace, lest it become soldered <note>clogged or fused</note> around the nozzles <term>nares</term> of the bellows and hinder the blast, causing the fire to burn less brightly. He has always been held in the number of excellent smelters who can temper the four elements. He tempers them who throws no more into the furnace than is appropriate for ore that partakes of the earth; who pours in water as often as the matter requires; who moderates the blast of the bellows with skill; and who throws the ore into the fire where it burns most brightly. Indeed, the master, by gradually pouring water into both parts of the furnace, should moisten the charcoals so that the finest parts of the ores may stick to them, which otherwise, agitated by the blast of the bellows and the force of the fires, would fly away and escape with the smoke.

But because the nature of ores to be smelted is diverse, smelters find it necessary to prepare the hearth sometimes high and sometimes low, and to place the pipe in which the nozzles of the bellows are located sometimes very inclined and sometimes only slightly. Likewise, they must breathe into the furnace a blast from the bellows that is sometimes gentle and sometimes vehement. For with ores that heat and melt quickly, smelters have need of a low hearth, a pipe placed with little inclination, and a gentle blast of the bellows; on the contrary, for those that heat and melt slowly, they need a high hearth, a pipe positioned with much inclination, and a vehement blast of the bellows. For these latter, they also need a very hot furnace in which slags have previously been re-smelted, or cakes melted from pyrites, or stones that melt easily in the fire have been cooked. Unless these things are done, the ores settling in the hearth of the furnace block the mouth and, as it were, suffocate it; which even the tiny metallic particles that settled while the ores were being washed are accustomed to do. Furthermore, large bellows should have wide nozzles; for if they are narrow, a great and powerful blast is breathed too tightly and sharply into the furnace, whereby the melted material is cooled and becomes soldered around the nozzles,

<summary>This page details the technical process of preparing and operating a smelting furnace, emphasizing the "tempering of the four elements" through precise control of heat, airflow, and additives like lead and pyrites. It describes the master smelter's role in adjusting the furnace geometry and blast strength according to the specific properties of different ores.</summary>
